news.title: Trump-Xi summit: How the Chinese leader's trip to Washington unfolded
news.text:
WASHINGTON/NEW YORK/TOKYO -- Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump have concluded their second formal summit of the year amid continuing tensions over tariffs, rare-earth minerals, artificial intelligence and more.

Four months after Trump traveled to Beijing in May, the two presidents met this time in Washington. The White House welcomed the Chinese leader in elaborate fashion, including a state dinner. Soon after Xi arrived in the Washington, the U.S. said the two sides had agreed to extend their trade truce, which had been due to expire Nov. 10.

But expectations of broader breakthroughs were modest, and the immediate results did little to shift perceptions. Trump and Xi are due to meet again at the APEC forum in Shenzhen in November, and at the G20 Summit in Miami in December.

Nikkei Asia followed Xi's visit live.

Further reading:

Here's how Xi's trip to the U.S. unfolded (Washington time):

Friday, Sept. 25

9:10 p.m. According to the U.S. ambassador to China, David Perdue, Trump warned Xi against providing support for Iran and received assurances, Reuters reports. In TV interviews earlier, Perdue said Trump reiterated that direct or indirect support for Tehran is "totally unacceptable."

7:20 p.m. Tech tensions continue to simmer. A bipartisan group of American lawmakers has introduced legislation to ban the U.S. government from equipping sensitive systems with Chinese-made components used to transmit data in AI data centers, Reuters reports.

The devices are known as optical transceivers. Supporters of the legislation say the devices could be used by Beijing to disrupt access to U.S. AI tools and the cloud, Reuters writes. The restriction would apply to optical transceivers made by China's Eoptolink and Zhongji Innolight. "We shouldn't rely on China for technologies that are essential to our national security," one of the lawmakers, Dave McCormick, says in a statement.

1:17 p.m. On his Truth Social platform, Trump bids farewell to Xi. "Much has been, and will be, accomplished," Trump writes. "I look forward to our next meeting!"

1:10 p.m. Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, board their plane at Joint Base Andrews, concluding their three-day visit to the United States.

12:15 p.m. Trump and Xi exchange a final handshake after a National Archives tour before Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, head to the airport.

11:20 a.m. Xi attends a tea ceremony with Trump. The Chinese leader says that he will welcome the U.S. president to come to China for the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in November and that he expects to meet with Trump again at the Group of 20 meeting in December. Trump says he will go to Shenzhen and that the two will "speak a lot." Xi says the prospects of relationships will get "brighter."

9:45 a.m. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer tells CNBC that details of the latest U.S.-China trade agreements will be released Monday.

Greer says Washington and Beijing reached deals covering a "subset" of non-sensitive goods that could receive more favorable trade terms, without specifying which products are covered or how tariffs might change.

8:50 a.m. Trump says on Truth Social that he had a "very productive meeting" with Xi and that "tremendous things will be happening." He does not provide further details.

7:20 a.m. The U.S. has yet to confirm details of yesterday's closed-door bilateral summit, but footage shows that Vice President JD Vance was among the officials in the room. This marks the potential 2028 presidential candidate's first known formal encounter with the Chinese leadership since taking office.

6:30 a.m. The coast guard of the Philippines, a U.S. treaty ally, accused China on Friday of obstructing a resupply mission to its troops in the South China Sea, Reuters reports. A spokesperson said dangerous maneuvers by Chinese vessels "put Filipino personnel at risk" and prevented the mission from being completed, although there were no collisions or injuries. This is the latest of numerous confrontations between Chinese and Philippine forces in the disputed waters.

4:30 a.m. At the National Archives, the last scheduled stop of Xi's visit before his departure from Washington, the leaders will have a chance to view some of the most important documents in American history, including the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. In addition, Trump has said they will see "artifacts testifying to the long and cherished relationship" between China and the U.S.

Analysts suggested to Reuters that Xi may want to see documents related to the U.S. decision to switch recognition to the People's Republic from Taiwan in 1979.

2:20 a.m. Taipei's Ministry of Foreign Affairs pushes back, after Xi told Trump that China wants the U.S. to uphold the "correct position" of opposing "Taiwan independence" and appeared to link the matter to overall relationship stability.

The Taiwanese ministry says Xi's comments are consistent with a pattern of "distorting facts" and stresses that the Chinese Communist Party "has no right to represent the Taiwanese people." It emphasizes democracy and insists Taiwan will continue to work with the U.S. and other partners to safeguard peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait.

2:00 a.m. As Xi's visit to Washington enters its final hours, economic pressures back home in China loom in the background. A recent high-profile tie-up deal between two major Chinese state-owned carmakers has raised the possibility of broader consolidation across the world's largest car market, analysts say, as Beijing's patience with chronic overcapacity in the industry wears thin.

Thursday, Sept. 24

11:30 p.m. Kolas Yotaka, a former spokesperson for Taiwan's presidential office, writes on X: "If 'one country, two systems' is the relationship China wants with Taiwan, then this new concept of "constructive strategic stability" is the relationship China wants with the U.S.," referring to the formulation for governing Hong Kong and Beijing's framing of its current ties with Washington. "Only difference? Taiwan doesn't accept China's terms. The U.S. just did. That's dangerous for Taiwan."

Yotaka, who is also an author, independent consultant and former legislator, suggests China is trying to box Trump in. It is "using this to demand the U.S. recognize its claim over Taiwan and delay arms sales -- or else it 'threatens' this new 'stability.' That would blow up the status quo."

9:50 p.m. According to the Trump administration, tomorrow's events will kick off when the presidents reconvene at the White House at 10:30 a.m. Trump and first lady Melania will have tea with Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan. Later in the morning, they will pay a visit to the National Archives, concluding Xi's state visit.

9:45 p.m. Here's some footage from the summit so far.

8:30 p.m. While dinner is underway, Chinese supporters and anti-China protesters are stationed outside the White House, separated by a few blocks. Groups of Hong Kongers, Uyghurs, Tibetans and Chinese rights activists waving Tibetan flags chant "Free Hong Kong" and "Stop the Uyghur genocide," while supporters play the Chinese national anthem.

8:15 p.m. Xi begins his remarks by wishing everyone a happy mid-autumn festival, a Chinese occasion celebrating family traditions and reunions.

Wearing a Mao suit, Xi says he and Trump had "sincere, in-depth exchanges" earlier today and came to an understanding on many issues, which the Chinese leader describes as new substance for "the constructive strategic relationship." He sprinkles historical events into his remarks, including "ping pong diplomacy" in 1971 during Richard Nixon's presidency, when the U.S. and China rebuilt the bilateral relationship. He also mentions that George Washington had a large collection of Chinese porcelain.

Xi highlights historic trade ties and the partnership to defeat Japan in World War II, saying the Sino-U.S. "friendship forged in blood and fire will live on for generations."

Closing out his remarks, Xi acknowledges Trump's goal of "making America great again," but also notes China's commitment to achieving "national rejuvenation."

"These two goals are both ambitious and can surely be mutually reinforcing," he says.

8:00 p.m. Hosting a state dinner with Xi's delegation and business leaders, Trump praises the historic ties between the two countries. He goes off script to point out the construction of the new White House ballroom and invites Xi to have a look. "If we had it, we would have way more than 1,000 people."

Trump gifts Xi a statue of a bald eagle, a national symbol of U.S., which he says was designed by himself and first lady Melania.

At Trump's table are tech leaders Elon Musk of Tesla, Jensen Huang of Nvidia, Lisa Su of AMD and Tim Cook of Apple.

4:20 p.m. According to a readout of a White House meeting earlier in the day published by state-run Xinhua News Agency, Trump and Xi confirmed they will support each other in hosting the APEC Economic Leaders' meeting in Shenzhen and the G20 Summit in Miami this year.

Xi said the two countries have held new rounds of trade talks and reached a new arrangement, which is good news for the industries, people on both sides and the global economy.

On Taiwan, Xi said China hopes the U.S. will uphold the "correct position" of opposing Taiwan independence, handle the Taiwan question with prudence, and lay a solid foundation for China-U.S. strategic cooperation and the development of bilateral relations.

"The fact that the two heads of state have visited each other in less than six months is unprecedented in the history of China-U.S. relations," the readout quotes Xi as saying. "President Trump and I have maintained communication through various means, working together to steer the ship of China-U.S. relations."

4:11p.m. Xi called for U.S. and China to keep artificial intelligence under human control during a White House meeting earlier in the day, Chinese state-run Xinhua News Agency reports.

According to the readout published by Xinhua, Xi discussed issues including trade, artificial intelligence and Taiwan with Trump.

On AI, Xi said both China and the U.S. are major powers in artificial intelligence. While there is competition, there is also the potential for cooperation. Both sides should leverage their respective strengths rather than adopt a defensive stance.

Xi called for the two parties to continue their dialogue on AI, exchanging views on its risks and benefits, and work together to prevent its misuse.

"Humans must remain in control over AI technology, adhering to a human-centered and benevolent approach," Xi said.

The two leaders also discussed the Middle East, Ukraine, Korea Peninsula and other geopolitical issues.

3:30 p.m. History and high culture, along with local specialties, will be on the menu for tonight's state dinner.

A blanc de noir from Schramsberg, the same vineyard whose sparkling wine was served in Beijing at U.S. President Richard Nixon and Premier Zhou Enlai's "Toast to Peace" in 1972, will be poured.

The first lady's office describes the menu as "bringing the culinary traditions of both nations together." The meal will begin with yellow squash veloute with mushroom fricassee, followed by sesame-crusted sea bass with braised baby bok choy. For dessert, vanilla cremeux served with ice cream using honey from the White House beehive.

Attendees will be serenaded by opera singer Christopher Macchio, a sharp contrast to R&B music artist Ne-Yo, whose hit song "Because of You" delighted Xi's wife, Peng Liyuan, in 2015.

Trump expressed his frustration this week that his controversial ballroom was not complete in time for Xi's visit.

1:40 p.m. Xi leaves the White House after shaking hands with Trump and climbing into his limo. Xi is scheduled to return in the evening for the state dinner.

1:15 p.m. Trump says he and Xi had a "great meeting" as the two leaders head to the Marine One helicopter for a brief tour of the White House grounds, according to The Associated Press.

The presidents walk together to the helipad, where Trump points out the presidential seal and shows off nearby construction on a planned White House ballroom. The U.S. president has repeatedly highlighted efforts to complete the helicopter landing area in time for Xi's visit.

12:45 p.m. China supports a return to dialogue and negotiations on Iran and hopes all sides can reach a comprehensive agreement, including on the nuclear issue, Xi Jinping says in a bilateral meeting with Trump, according to state-owned Xinhua News Agency.

Xi says China has sought to help de-escalate tensions and believes the sovereignty and security of all nations should be respected.

12:30 p.m. Xi says China will send two giant pandas to Zoo Atlanta as a goodwill gesture, after Beijing recalled four pandas from the zoo in 2024 amid rising U.S.-China tensions.

China and Zoo Atlanta announced in April that male Ping Ping and female Fu Shuang would come to the U.S. under a panda conservation agreement. In the welcoming remarks, Xi says the pair will arrive at their new Atlanta home "in a few days" and calls panda exchanges an "envoy of friendship."

11:50 a.m. The summit schedule includes no joint news conference, and it remains unclear whether Trump and Xi will take questions from U.S. or Chinese reporters, according to the AP.

That marks a departure from Xi's 2015 White House visit, when he and President Barack Obama held a joint news conference in the Rose Garden. After opening remarks, each leader answered questions from both American and Chinese reporters.

10:45 a.m. In welcoming remarks delivered after the playing of the U.S. and Chinese national anthems, Trump says the two sides have made "tremendous strides" and will be discussing security, technology and "super intelligence," his term for AI. He adds that both countries are working to balance trade, including "new market access" for American farmers.

Invoking historic ties between China and the U.S., including their alliance during WWII, the U.S. president says they will focus on "common interests."

Xi, speaking at the White House for the first time since 2015, stresses the importance of partnership between the world's two largest economies, as well as the need for mutual respect and trust, while strengthening cooperation and communication.

"Without our cooperation between the U.S. and China, it'd be hard to solve many of the world's problems," he says.

10:30 a.m. Demonstrators are peacefully marching from the Chinese Embassy toward Capitol Hill in protest against Beijing's cultural repression in Tibet. In July, Tibetan activist Lobsang Palden self-immolated in front of the United Nations building and died from severe burns. The incident happened a week after an "ethnic unity" law came into effect in China. The legislation promotes integration across the country's 55 ethnic groups through various policies, but critics see it as an instrument to further repress minorities.

This week, a Tibet independence march was held in front of the U.N. headquarters in New York. Fifteen other Tibetan demonstrators have marched from New York through Philadelphia and toward Washington to honor Palden.

Chinese authorities have imposed policies of forced assimilation in Tibet, restricting the use of the Tibetan language and subjecting individuals to arbitrary detention. Rights activists say the Chinese Communist Party is systematically separating Tibetan children from their families to erase Tibetan identity, but the Chinese government has denied accusations of cultural repression.

10:15 a.m. The U.S. president and first lady welcome Xi and his wife to the White House.

9:12 a.m. World financial markets remained on edge on Thursday after concerns about the Iran war and inflation pain had triggered the sharpest sell-off in U.S. Treasurys and other benchmark government bonds since last year's "Liberation Day" turmoil, Reuters reported.

Bond yields were nudging higher again as U.S. trading began after oil prices had moved back above $105 a barrel and as traders waited on what could be a tense meeting between Trump and Xi in Washington later.

The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield -- the benchmark of the $29 trillion Treasury market that anchors pricing for virtually all financial assets globally --touched a new post-financial-crisis high of 5.12%, while the 30-year yield climbed to 5.44%, its highest since 2004.

8:00 a.m. Trump starts the day off with a Truth Social post, suggesting he will discuss AI with Xi.

"A big day with President Xi of China. Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China's position also," he writes.

"Our guardrail is the DOJ!" Trump adds, referring to the Department of Justice but not elaborating on what he means.

6:35 a.m. While the U.S. and Chinese leaders meet in Washington, trade tensions over what many consider China's industrial overcapacity are simmering elsewhere. The head of Germany's auto industry association, VDA, has explicitly endorsed new tariffs on China for the first time, Reuters reports, citing German media. Hildegard Mueller told newspaper Handelsblatt that trade countermeasures could be adopted when competition has been distorted beyond a certain extent, including cases of "proven unfair behavior."

While China's trade with the U.S. has declined, it has stepped up exports to Europe and Southeast Asia, and Germany's leaders have been raising alarm. Chancellor Friedrich Merz recently said China "deliberately" combines market forces with state subsidies, overcapacity, aggressive pricing and an undervalued currency.

European companies in China this week urged Beijing to address such concerns ahead of crucial talks with the bloc next month.

4:50 a.m. According to the schedule shared by the U.S., Trump will welcome Xi and his wife to the White House at 10 a.m. Shortly afterward, the leaders will observe an arrival ceremony, before delivering brief remarks, exchanging gifts and participating in military reviews.

At 11:30 a.m., with the pageantry out of the way, Trump and Xi will start a closed bilateral meeting in the Oval Office. Only half an hour is reserved for this, before they shift to an expanded meeting in the Cabinet Room at noon.

At 2 p.m., Trump is due to turn to his own briefings and meetings, until the leaders reconvene at 6:45 p.m. They are to deliver further remarks before tucking into a state dinner with business leaders.

3:45 a.m. China's Ministry of Defense calls for maintaining "stable and sound" relations with the U.S. military, while urging Washington to be "extremely cautious" about arms sales to Taiwan.

2:00 a.m. Major U.S. media outlets avoided broadcasting Trump's grand welcome for Xi, according to reports, as his administration feuds with the press. Trump recently sought to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from reporting from the White House, accusing them of reporting "lies." Fox News, which is generally friendly to Trump, also refrained from showing Wednesday's ceremony. A federal judge subsequently ordered Trump to restore White House access for journalists from the three affected outlets, saying the ban was likely unconstitutional, Reuters reported.

1:30 a.m. Taiwan's cabinet spokesperson, Michelle Lee, says Taipei expresses its "gratitude" for long-standing U.S. support.

"Regarding all efforts conducive to stabilizing the regional situation and managing the risks that authoritarian expansion might bring, we view them positively and continue to cooperate with the U.S. at various levels," she says, regarding the Trump-Xi meeting, according to Reuters.

"In fact, we continue to maintain close contact with the U.S. to stay informed of relevant developments."

12:35 a.m. Minoru Kihara, Japan's chief cabinet secretary and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's top aide, tells reporters in Tokyo that he will "continue to monitor the situation" at the Trump-Xi summit "closely with keen interest," amid Japan's own tensions with Beijing.

He stresses the significance of talks between Takaichi and Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly earlier this week. "With the upcoming U.S.-China summit in mind, they exchanged views on various issues concerning China including economic security, and agreed to continue to closely cooperate," he said.

Wednesday, Sept. 23

11:45 p.m. The European Chamber of Commerce in China applauds the extension of the trade truce between Washington and Beijing, saying that without it, "the implementation of the planned export controls on rare earths would have a crippling impact on industry."

However, it raises several concerns, including uncertainty over what will happen after the new expiry date of Jan. 10.

"The extension does not address underlying challenges companies experience when it comes to applying for both single and general export licenses" for rare earths, it adds. The chamber flags "a lack of coordination" between Chinese commerce and customs authorities, inconsistent disclosure requirements and "a lack of clarity as to why some applications are unsuccessful."

11:00 p.m. As the U.S. was preparing to welcome Xi, Chinese human rights activist Shi Tingfu died in prison in the country's northwestern region of Xinjiang on Tuesday, according to the Chinese-language website Rights Defense Network (RDN).

Shi, an outspoken advocate of freedom and democracy from Nanjing who supported the 1989 Tiananmen protests, was detained by Xinjiang police in January 2024 and later sentenced to three years in jail for "picking quarrels and provoking trouble." He was expected to be released in about four months.

The death of the 67-year-old activist underscores questions over whether Trump will press Xi on human rights issues in their meeting on Thursday, beyond raising the cases of two Americans held by Beijing.

Shi's conviction was due to passing information to overseas media about fruit farmers in the western Xinjiang city of Aral, or Alar, lodging grievances against Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps, a state-run paramilitary organization and corporate conglomerate.

The Network of Chinese Human Rights Defenders said it could not definitively confirm that his death resulted from inadequate medical care. He suffered from multiple health conditions, including high blood pressure, pneumonia and asthma.

But according to RDN, his family said he had appeared to be in good condition and did not mention feeling unwell during a visit not long ago, "raising concerns about the circumstances of his sudden death."

On another front, the Tibet Action Institute reports that China has been enforcing a "complete information blackout across Tibet" following catastrophic landslides and floods at the border with Nepal last month.

"Xi Jinping's regime tried to make Tibet invisible after the devastating border floods," said Tenzin Dorjee, the institute's research and advocacy director, by "blocking journalists, silencing victims, and censoring the internet -- all to mask the truth of its occupation and colonization of Tibet." She called on Trump to press Xi to allow access and end the "relentless repression" of Tibetans.

10:30 p.m. The White House has posted a short video clip of Trump's welcome for Xi.

View post on X

10:00 p.m. Days ahead of his U.S. visit, Xi wrote back to nearly 100 students from 10 U.S. universities who had been in China for an exchange program, according to the state-owned Xinhua News Agency. He urged them to foster bilateral ties.

Yet, even as leaders trade diplomatic overtures, academic and people-to-people exchanges between the two superpowers remain severely chilled after years of deepening political mistrust. The pipeline for American scholars going to China has nearly dried up. And the number of U.S. students studying in China has dropped sharply from roughly 11,000 in 2019 to fewer than 2,000, with most concentrated in short-term undergraduate programs, according to the U.S.-China Education Trust.

At the same time, Chinese students are increasingly shunning American universities amid tighter visa restrictions and heightened immigration scrutiny. The number of Chinese students on American campuses fell from a peak of more than 370,000 in the 2019-2020 academic year to nearly 266,000 by 2024-2025.

8:30 p.m. According to a list shared with media, the welcome ceremony for Xi featured: a 100-foot red carpet; a salute battery; a 21-person honor cordon; a pair of three-person color teams with the U.S. and Chinese flags; a U.S. Air Force band playing fanfare and the countries' national anthems; 3x5 platoons from each service; two B1 flyovers; and flower presenters.

6:20 p.m. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News that he and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng agreed to extend a trade truce through Jan. 10, two months beyond its Nov. 10 expiration date.

5:41 p.m. Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington to a rare tarmac welcome from President Donald Trump, who breaks with convention by greeting his counterpart planeside.

Trump and first lady Melania Trump are to take part in an arrival ceremony for Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, kicking off a three-day state visit.

4:30 p.m. Before President Donald Trump's tariffs, China bought about half of U.S. soybean exports. Since then, shipments have fallen sharply, from nearly $18 billion in 2022 to $3 billion in 2025, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data.

The decline has helped Brazil and Argentina gain market share. Brazil exported a record 108.7 million metric tons of soybeans in 2025, up 11.7% from a year earlier, with about 80% headed to China, according to the National Association of Cereal Exporters.

"No one can replace the Chinese market," Dave Walton, vice president of the American Soybean Association and an Iowa farmer, tells the Associated Press. Walton says he hopes U.S. tariffs are removed, adding: "We think of Xi as a friend to American agriculture."

3:30 p.m. Secretary of State Marco Rubio says the U.S. and China have a responsibility to engage at the highest levels, calling regular contact between the world's two largest economies "responsible statecraft."

"The idea that we would not interact with them at the highest levels is irresponsible. It's outrageous. We have to," Rubio tells reporters on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, according to the Associated Press.

His comments come hours before President Donald Trump is set to welcome Chinese President Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews in a rare tarmac ceremony.

2:00 p.m. Security in Washington is being beefed up as Chinese diaspora groups plan welcome events and activist groups prepare demonstrations in conjunction with tomorrow's summit.

Road closures around the White House are already in place. The U.S. Secret Service, which is leading security for Xi's visit, says it is committed to ensuring the safety of foreign heads of state who are in the U.S.

Chinese, Hong Kong, Tibetan and Uyghur activists say they expect several thousand people to protest on Thursday.

"We're all protesting for a simple reason ... because our people who used to say these things, who used to organize these demonstrations back at home, are now locked up behind bars in prisons, in concentration camps and are stripped away from their political freedom and rights," says Joey Siu, a Hong Kong human rights activist.

Activist groups clashed with Chinese government supporters when Xi visited San Francisco for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in 2023.

The Secret Service says it is prepared to manage any demonstrations to ensure that freedom of assembly and speech are expressed "safely."

"If individuals or groups decide to act unlawfully, plans have been put in place to address them efficiently and safely," the Secret Service says in a statement.

1:05 p.m. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says he has held "substantive discussions" with China's He Lifeng on the bilateral economic relationship ahead of Trump's summit with Xi.

View post on X

11:30 a.m. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng again hours before Xi is set to arrive in Washington.

"We have some unfinished business from Sunday," Bessent tells reporters here when asked what prompted this meeting, his second talk with He this week.

"We want strategic stability, but it has to be based in reciprocity and fairness," Bessent also says.

During closed-door negotiations Sunday at JPMorgan headquarters in Manhattan, the two sides agreed to carve out "nonsensitive" goods from future tariff actions.

7:40 a.m. There are signs of a generational shift among Americans in how they look at their country's biggest competitor. Younger and Democratic-leaning Americans, in particular, are warming up to the idea of building closer ties with China rather than decoupling, studies show.

A survey by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs released this week found 57% of American respondents favored engaging with China, the highest level since 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic. The same poll found that Americans themselves perceive global respect for the U.S. to have declined over the last 10 years, while most respondents said respect for China was either about the same or had increased.

According to the Ronald Reagan Institute Summer Survey, 93% of Americans aged 65 and above expressed concern about Chinese espionage, compared with just 62% of those aged 18 to 29. The younger set was also less likely to worry about a potential military conflict over Taiwan, Chinese purchases of U.S. land and China's role in fentanyl flows.

Data on how Chinese citizens view America is far less accessible, though recent downtrends in Chinese visiting and studying in the U.S. indicate caution along with the effects of rising visa restrictions and tighter immigration rules.

7:00 a.m. Xi is heading stateside at a time when China's global image has improved, at least in relation to the U.S.

A report by Gallup published in April shows that China surpassed the U.S. in global approval ratings in 2025. A median 36% approved of Chinese leadership versus 31% for the U.S. -- the widest gap in China's favor in nearly 20 years.

This appears to reflect not only Xi's efforts to portray Beijing as a responsible power but also deteriorating views of America in Trump's second term. "Overall, China's move ahead of the U.S. more broadly reflects a decline in U.S. ratings rather than an increase in China's ratings," the report says.

A more recent survey by the Pew Research Center, conducted across 37 economies, found that a median of 51% of respondents had a favorable view of China. Feelings toward the country were warmest in Southeast Asia, Africa and Latin America, where China has deepened its trade ties in recent years.

Confidence in both Trump and Xi was generally low, according to Pew, though people from 22 countries viewed Xi more favorably of the two. Respondents in only eight countries, including Japan and Israel, expressed significantly greater confidence in Trump than Xi.

Still, the Pew survey found the U.S. government ranks higher than Beijing in terms of respect for personal freedom.

6:30 a.m. This will be Xi's first official state visit to the U.S. since 2015, and his first time setting foot on American soil since the APEC forum in 2023. Much has changed for both countries over the past decade -- key context for how the two administrations may approach relations.

In the U.S., a booming stock market fueled by artificial intelligence-related investments has supercharged wealth among high-income households. But middle- to low-income families face higher costs of living, exacerbated by elevated energy bills due to Trump's war against Iran.

The 20% richest Americans now account for 60% of personal spending, according to Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics.

Polls suggest that the affordability problem has eroded Trump's popularity. One released this week by Reuters/Ipsos found that only 32% of Americans approved of the president's job performance, the lowest of his career, while just 17% approved of his handling of living costs.

There is no publicly available polling on Xi's performance atop China's Communist Party state. Still, there are signs of brewing discontent due to labor market pains. Youth unemployment hit a record of 18.9% in August, amid widespread adoption of AI.

China has cemented its grip on global manufacturing with a record trade surplus of over $1 trillion, despite Trump's repeated attempts to loosen that hold with tariffs since his first term in 2018. And Chinese companies are making rapid technological advances. Yet the country also faces a two-speed economy: a yearslong property slump has dented family wealth and suppressed retail spending, while overall official growth rates continue to trend downward.

6:10 a.m. Here's the scene at Joint Base Andrews in the wee hours of Wednesday, ahead of Trump's welcome for Xi.

6:00 a.m. At a forum in Sydney earlier, experts in Asian and military affairs offered cautionary assessments.

John Aquilino, a retired commander of the U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, said China is conducting the largest military buildup since World War II. "Their industrial base is in a wartime footing. They are cranking out ships, submarines and airplanes like it's their day job. That is for only one reason, and that is for the PRC to change the current world order in ways that benefit China at the expense of all of us," he said.

Aquilino emphasized a need for the U.S. to work with allies on economic alternatives and deterrence. On the upcoming summit, he said the direction of conversations about Taiwan "absolutely concerns me." Reuters reported this week that Xi is likely to push Trump to halt new arms sales to Taipei.

Kurt Campbell, a former U.S. deputy secretary of state and co-founder of The Asia Group, said at the same event that Xi is trying to "reduce the confidence in Taiwan in the United States" by framing "how to think about Taiwan and resisting arms sales."

Lai I-Chung, president of the Prospect Foundation think tank, said Taiwan will be watching the summit "very closely" but stressed that the island democracy's fate will "not be determined by the negotiation between those two powers."

5:45 a.m. Tesla CEO Elon Musk says Xi is a "great leader" in an interview aired by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV. The billionaire, who is reportedly due to join Thursday's state dinner with the two presidents in Washington, says China has "prospered immensely" during Xi's time in power.

Musk has repeatedly praised China in recent weeks, while denying rumors that he is looking to break off Tesla's operations there.

5:15 a.m. A commentary in the Communist Party's People's Daily presents a broadly upbeat view of the summit. "The China-U.S. relationship is the most important and complex bilateral relationship in the world, and head-of-state diplomacy serves as the 'guiding star' of this relationship," it reads. It repeatedly emphasizes "constructive strategic stability," a framing of the superpower relationship that emerged at the May summit.

In a separate piece in the People's Daily, China's ambassador to the U.S., Xie Feng, lays out boundaries. "China's sovereignty, security, and development interests cannot be violated, and four red lines -- the Taiwan question, democracy and human rights, development paths and systems, and development rights -- cannot be challenged."

5:05 a.m. Xi is en route for Washington, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reports. The announcement says he is accompanied by his wife, Peng Liyuan, along with top aide Cai Qi and Foreign Minister Wang Yi, "among others."

He is scheduled to land in the early evening at Joint Base Andrews, where he is due to be greeted by Trump himself -- a rare diplomatic courtesy.

In a note, Oxford Economics says that the trip is "a sign the U.S.-China relationship is becoming more predictable." Yet, the advisory firm says both sides are "buying time."

"China wants to preserve export access while reducing external technology dependence. The U.S. wants to limit near-term supply-chain disruption and build manufacturing capacity at home. Economic interdependence is difficult to unwind, and both sides need time to build credible substitutes."

The analysts predict "narrow" and "reversible" outcomes, including limited tariff relief, a potential expansion of commitments to purchase farm goods and aircraft, and pledges to cooperate on issues like AI safety and Iran. "That would leave the thornier issues around tech rivalry, transshipments and Taiwan unresolved."

news.title: US Supreme Court rejects a Trump-backed Missouri congressional map for the third time
news.text: JEFFERSON CITY: The Supreme Court on Friday turned away an attempt to use a new Missouri congressional map backed by President Donald Trump, putting an end to a long-running legal dispute as absentee voting is underway in the midterm elections.The justices halted a federal appeals court ruling that would have revived the Republican-friendly map for the November elections, which will determine control of Congress. There were no noted dissents.The Supreme Court instead let stand a decision by the Missouri Supreme Court, which ruled earlier this month that a citizen petition prevents the new map from being used unless first approved by voters in a November referendum. The decision means Missouri residents will vote under the same congressional districts used in the 2024 and 2022 elections.“At this late date, ordering reversion to the 2025 map in the midst of an ongoing election would usher in electoral chaos,” the high court wrote in an unsigned opinion. “The District Court and Court of Appeals should not enjoin or otherwise prohibit the use of the 2022 map in the 2026 congressional election in Missouri.”Republicans had hoped the new House map — which already was used in the August primaries — could help them win an additional seat as part of a nationwide redistricting battle pushed by Trump to gain an edge in the midterms.The new map had targeted a district held by longtime Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.“I think my reelection prospects shot up significantly,” a jubilant Cleaver said after the Supreme Court ruling.A panel of the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals had ruled Monday that switching districts between the primary and general elections would violate the U.S. Constitution. The panel directed a district judge to bar Missouri from using anything other than the new map but delayed the order's effect until next Monday to allow time for an appeal to the Supreme Court.Republican Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins described the high court's decision as “a disappointing blow to representative democracy,” but added, “I appreciate the final clarity.”The legal wrangling has caused confusion for more than a million potential Missouri voters — nearly 1 in 4 statewide — who were shifted from one district to another, resulting in different candidates on their ballots. Absentee voting began Tuesday under the 2022 congressional districts. Thousands of ballots already had been mailed, and some already have been cast.A decision from the Supreme Court is “a big sigh of relief," said Kansas City election director Shawn Kieffer. He added, "We just want it over, so we can do our job properly.”.Republican redistricting focused on Kansas CityRepublicans currently hold six of Missouri's eight House districts. At the urging of Trump and Republican Gov. Mike Kehoe, Missouri lawmakers last September passed revised districts that were intended to help them win seven seats in the midterms.The redistricting significantly reshaped a Kansas City-based district held by Cleaver. It shed parts of Kansas City to neighboring districts with Republican incumbents and stretched the remainder of Cleaver's 5th Congressional District far eastward into rural Republican areas.The result was about 59% of potential voters were new to the district, according to an Associated Press estimate. The ripple effects also shifted some voters in most of Missouri's other congressional districts.Cleaver was unopposed in the Democratic primary. Republican state Sen. Rick Brattin won a six-way Republican primary under the revised districts. They remain the candidates for the general election, even though the district boundaries have reverted to their prior lines.Cleaver said the court ruling affirms the people's right to use to referendum petitions against state legislative actions they don't like.“We just received a healthy dose of encouragement that the voice of people in the United States still matters," he said.Brattin was a plaintiff, along with Republican Rep. Bob Onder and two other voters, in a federal lawsuit that led to the 8th Circuit's ruling and the last two appeals to the Supreme Court.Brattin denounced Friday's decision as “a travesty,” calling the switching of districts after the primary “the most unprecedented form of voter disenfranchisement in American history.”.Missouri's redistricting prompted a big legal fightAt least 16 lawsuits have been filed in state and federal courts related to Missouri's congressional redistricting. The battle has been the longest and most complex among roughly a dozen states that sought to change their U.S. House districts over the past year.Missouri's new map survived most of the lawsuits, including ones contending that mid-decade redistricting violated the state constitution and that the new districts ran afoul of requirements to be compact. In one case, the Missouri Supreme Court allowed the new districts to be used while election officials worked to verify petition signatures seeking to put the map to a statewide vote.Hoskins waited until the legal deadline on Aug. 4 — the day the new districts were used in the primaries — to reject the petition. He asserted referendum petitions aren't allowed for congressional redistricting.The Missouri Supreme Court ruled Sept. 3 that the referendum petition was valid. It ordered Hoskins not to use the new map and to instead use the districts adopted in 2022, after the last census. The U.S. Supreme Court let that ruling stand on Sept. 8. But minutes later, U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark issued a conflicting order in favor of the new map.The U.S. Supreme Court on Sept. 10 blocked Clark's order from taking effect. That day, the Missouri Supreme Court held Hoskins temporarily in contempt for telling local election authorities to use the new map after Clark's order.But that wasn't the end of the matter. The 8th Circuit, hearing an appeal of Clark's blocked order, ruled in favor of the Trump-backed map Monday. That's what led to the latest decision from the U.S. Supreme Court.Richard von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians Missouri, said the group was pressing forward with its campaign to persuade voters to permanently reject the new map in the November referendum.“We have said from the beginning, people, not politicians will be the final deciders on this DC power grab," he said in a statement..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Saudi Arabia ‘has not ruled out’ developing nuclear weapons – WaPo
news.text:
Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing nuclear weapons, according to a classified US intelligence assessment that has fueled concerns in Congress over President Donald Trump’s nuclear cooperation agreement with Riyadh, the Washington Post reported on Friday.

The assessment was included in classified documents provided to lawmakers as they review the landmark agreement, US officials told the newspaper. The State Department reportedly provided a separate assessment that was more confident in Saudi assurances and the safeguards built into the deal.

Signed in July, the so-called Section 123 agreement lays the legal groundwork for American companies to participate in tens of billions of dollars’ worth of civilian nuclear projects in Saudi Arabia. The Trump administration has argued that the arrangement will strengthen nonproliferation standards while preventing Riyadh from turning to Russia or China for nuclear cooperation.

However, the agreement creates a potential pathway for Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium domestically. Enrichment would initially be capped below 5%, but could later rise to as much as 20% following additional studies and written approval by Washington and Riyadh. Uranium enriched to that level remains below weapons grade, but substantially reduces the additional work required to reach weapons-grade concentrations.

The pact also does not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Additional Protocol, which provides inspectors with broader access and additional tools for detecting undeclared nuclear activity. Instead, Washington and Riyadh have negotiated a separate bilateral safeguards arrangement.

A group of Democratic senators led by Ed Markey and Jeff Merkley warned Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday that the deal could ultimately give Riyadh “the means to enrich uranium and possibly develop nuclear weapons.” Merkley told the Post that Saudi Arabia’s insistence on retaining the option of domestic enrichment raised questions over whether its ambitions were entirely civilian.

The State Department rejected suggestions that Washington was facilitating a military program, telling the newspaper that the US “does not and will not support a Saudi nuclear weapon program.” Saudi Energy Minister Abdulaziz bin Salman has likewise insisted that Riyadh’s program will be “peaceful” and developed with “the highest levels of responsibility and transparency.”

The intelligence assessment has added to longstanding concerns over Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s 2018 statement that Riyadh would seek an atomic bomb if Iran acquired one.

“Without a doubt, if Iran developed a nuclear bomb, we would follow suit as soon as possible,” he said at the time.

Lawmakers have also contrasted the Saudi agreement with the much stricter 2015 Iran nuclear deal, which capped Tehran’s uranium enrichment at 3.67% for 15 years. Trump withdrew the US from that deal during his first term, claiming it was not strict enough to prevent Tehran from obtaining a bomb.

The Saudi agreement was formally submitted to Congress on August 24 and is undergoing a 90-day review. Lawmakers can seek to block it, although overriding a presidential veto would require a two-thirds majority in both chambers.
news.summary:
A classified US intelligence assessment has fueled concerns over President Donald Trump’s civilian nuclear deal with Riyadh

news.title: Bipartisan Senators Urge Trump: Do Not Bring Putin to Miami
news.text:
A bipartisan group of 14 US senators is urging President Donald Trump to withdraw his invitation to Russian President Vladimir Putin for the December G20 summit in Miami, warning that welcoming the Kremlin leader to US soil risks legitimizing Moscow while Russia continues its full-scale war against Ukraine.

In a sharply worded Sept. 24 letter, the lawmakers said Putin “bears sole responsibility” for launching the invasion and argued that his participation in the summit would come as Russian forces continue striking Ukrainian cities and civilian infrastructure.

“Allowing him to participate in a G20 Summit in the United States raises serious concerns about legitimizing and normalizing a government that continues to attack Ukrainian civilian targets every day,” the senators wrote.

The bipartisan push was led by Republican Senator Roger Wicker, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, and Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen, ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. The letter was also signed by Mitch McConnell, John Cornyn, Michael Bennet, Chris Coons, Richard Blumenthal, Sheldon Whitehouse, Jerry Moran, Tim Kaine, Thom Tillis, John Curtis, Ruben Gallego and Alan Armstrong.

The senators also pointed to Russia’s military cooperation with Iran and what they described as hybrid operations across Europe, arguing that Washington should maintain political and economic pressure on Moscow rather than offer Putin a prominent international platform.

They further urged the Trump administration to prevent sanctioned senior Russian officials from entering the US for G20-related events.

The congressional pressure comes as Washington simultaneously pursues renewed diplomacy over the war.

President Volodymyr Zelensky said the United States has proposed a new trilateral meeting at the technical level involving Ukraine, the US and Russia, with the United Arab Emirates floated as a possible venue.

Putin, however, cast doubt on whether Moscow would resume negotiations. Speaking Friday, he said Russia would reconsider its position following recent Ukrainian strikes inside Russia and claimed Moscow would decide its next steps according to what it sees as Russian interests.
news.summary: A bipartisan group of 14 US senators is pressing President Donald Trump to rescind Vladimir Putin’s invitation to the December G20 summit in Miami and maintain pressure on Moscow.

news.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russian attacks force closure of Ukraine’s largest steelmaker
news.text:
The world’s second biggest steelmaker, ArcelorMittal, has closed Ukraine’s largest steel plant, highlighting the growing economic toll from Russian airstrikes. The multinational ⁠said on Friday it had told ​the Ukrainian government that “safe and sustainable” operations were not possible after four strikes in five weeks caused extensive damage and killed five workers at the plant in Kryvyi Rih in central Ukraine. The decision is another blow to Ukraine’s steel sector, which used to account for 15% of the country’s exports ⁠but has come under pressure from Russian attacks and restrictions from the EU. Russia has increased airstrikes on Ukraine in recent months using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones that have hit businesses, logistics networks, Black Sea port facilities and civilian infrastructure.

The ArcelorMittal closure comes as the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said ⁠on Friday that Russia was constantly expanding its attacks on infrastructure Ukrainians relied on for daily life, such as datacentres and warehouses. “There were also drone strikes today on a warehouse used by McDonald’s. An attack drone – against ordinary food products … American and other businesses, datacentres, internet providers – for Russia, ordinary life in and of itself is simply a target,” Zelenskyy said on X. “All of this undermines people’s ability to stay connected, study, and work.”

The Ukrainian president said the European Union and the International Monetary Fund understood the importance of helping Kyiv finance its budget deficit and ⁠defence spending. Ukraine is seeking ⁠an additional $27bn from partners this year for defence, saying the cost of the war has risen. Kyiv has asked to ⁠bring forward part of a loan from the EU. Zelenskyy said Ukraine needed to order ​drones in October and November or ‌it would face challenges ‌at the start of next year. “Everyone understands that Ukraine cannot be alone, and that more ‌investment is needed in Ukrainian-made drones and missiles,” he told reporters in a WhatsApp briefing.

Zelenskyy has asked Donald Trump to press China’s leader to use Beijing’s influence over Moscow to get Russia to end the war. On Friday, Zelenskyy told reporters he had not yet heard from the White House about Trump’s talks with Chinese president Xi Jinping but expected to learn the outcome soon. Zelenskyy was in the US this week on a trip coinciding with the UN general assembly. He met Trump on Tuesday. Nato countries have called China a “decisive enabler” of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s invasion.

Meanwhile, Putin has claimed Russia is not preparing for “any kind” of conflict with Europe. Putin made his comments after warnings from some European Nato members of potential Russian attacks on the alliance’s territory, including Denmark’s defence intelligence service, which this week warned of a “low but growing risk” that Russia could launch long-range strikes on Nato infrastructure supporting Ukraine. Putin said Russia had “no real motive” to escalate tensions and criticised European countries that have suggested otherwise. “I want to emphasise once again: we are not preparing for any kind of hostilities with Europe,” he said.

Senior European officials have sought to play down fears that ⁠potential election victories by Ukraine-sceptic parties in France and Germany could undermine support for Kyiv. Speaking to Reuters on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, officials acknowledged risks posed by shifting electoral tides but said support ⁠for Kyiv would endure. Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys acknowledged elections were one of the factors shaping calculations about future support but said backing for Ukraine would endure even if some countries became less committed: “If someone additionally will fall from those ⁠strong supporters of Ukraine, others will stand because this is in our interest.” Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said concerns about elections should not distract Europe from Ukraine’s immediate needs. “The main thing is not only about elections, it’s about Ukraine,” he said.

A bipartisan group of 14 senators is urging Trump to rescind the invitation to Russian President Vladimir Putin to attend the G20 summit to be held in Florida in December. “President Putin bears sole responsibility for launching Russia’s full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine. Allowing him to participate in a G20 Summit in the United States raises serious concerns about legitimising and normalising a government that continues to attack Ukrainian civilian targets every day,” the senators wrote in a letter. Among those who signed the letter are Jeanne Shaheen, Mitch McConnell, Roger Wicker, and Chris Coons.

news.title: Welch urged to do more than apologize for Benton harassment case
news.text:
Last month, House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch told WGN Political Editor Tahman Bradley during an interview, “I’m going to apologize for making her feel uncomfortable.”

The woman he was referring to was a district office worker for former Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield, who who quit after she said she was sexually harassed. The woman also told the Chicago Tribune that Welch had sent “heart-eye” emojis to her mobile phone in response to photos and said when she reached out to Welch about her future career plans, he suggested that they meet at a bar in his favorite suburban steakhouse. All of that, she said made her feel quite uncomfortable.

“I’m going to own that. I regret it, and I want to apologize to her,” Welch told Bradley. “I sincerely want to apologize to her because it was never my intent to make her or anyone feel uncomfortable.”

So, I reached out to the young former staffer through an approved intermediary to ask if Welch had ever apologized to her.

“No, he’s never apologized to me,” she replied.

When I asked whether she thinks Welch “should” apologize, the former staffer said there was something else he should do along with an apology: “I think I’d like to hear how he plans to improve the culture along with the apology,” she said. “Empty apology for his actions alone would just be awkward,” she continued.

I showed the back-and-forth between me and the intermediary to several House Democrats. Most said the culture change was more important.

Rep. Kelly Cassidy, D-Chicago, who has been a Welch critic, had this to say: “I agree with her perspective. A personal apology is empty unless backed with significant action. We need to fix the policies and procedures that failed her, but also the culture that led to the harm in the first place.”

Cassidy also didn’t expect that a Welch-style apology would be sufficient: “I have issues with apologies that focus on the feelings of the victim as opposed to his actions.”

“I’ve always been less interested in apologies and more concerned with fixing problems,” said Rep. Mary Beth Canty, D-Arlington Heights, who also chairs the House Women’s Caucus.

“I think her comment that she’d like substantive cultural changes and not just an apology makes sense and is wise,” said Rep. Anna Moeller, D-Elgin. “From what I’ve heard, the working group assembled by the speaker is taking the task seriously, and I think the caucus will be looking for substantive proposals to help ensure that district staff are protected. I think if the speaker knew that she’d like a direct apology he would provide one.”

Well, he knows now.

Rep. Will Guzzardi, D-Chicago, is a member of Welch’s leadership team: “All of us, especially those of us in leadership, bear responsibility for the workplace culture in Springfield that’s too often toxic and harmful. We need a plan to make things better. I’ve been talking with my colleagues throughout the summer, and I’m hopeful that we can come together in veto session with some concrete steps to improve our processes and keep our people safe.”

Rep. Ann Stava, D-Naperville, noted that the working group got off to a very rocky start: “[Welch’s] response was to formally assign people to a working group to ‘study the issue.’ Multiple members who were assigned declined to join for reasons they specified publicly.”

Stava also said that she hadn’t decided whether to vote for Welch in January, and warned, “I do not look kindly on the fact that he has not personally apologized to the original victim or the subsequent victims to my knowledge.”

In my own opinion, Welch should follow through on both of his public promises: Genuinely apologize and improve the staff working environment.

Instead, the House Democrats have gone on offense against the Republican candidate running against Benton’s successor, Gabby Shanahan.

Benton was succeeded by one of his former district office employees, who said she witnessed Benton’s sexual harassment but didn’t report it because the young staffer asked her not to. The Republicans have sharply and repeatedly criticized appointed Rep. Jessica Dixon Heitman, D-Plainfield, for turning a blind eye to what happened.

The Democrats are now trying to turn the Republican attacks back against the GOP candidate Shanahan.

“Gabby Shanahan’s biggest backer is a top Trump ally,” the narrator says in the Democratic streaming ad as photos of President Donald Trump, House Speaker Mike Johnson and Vice President JD Vance appear beside Shanahan, according to my associate Isabel Miller.

“We don’t need another politician like Shanahan who will look the other way” the ad states.

Clever, considering that’s just what Welch did with Benton.

Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.

news.title: Barbados PM wants region to rmain zone of peace
news.text:
UNITED NATIONS, Sept 24, CMC – Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley Thursday called for the Caribbean region to remain a zone of peace and that there should be no acceptance o the region “becoming a theatre for confrontation or for the unilateral and unjustified use of force”.

In an address to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), Mottley said that it is also necessary for political leaders in the Caribbean to play a pivotal role in ensuring that the region remains peaceful and progressive.

She said that the situation in the French-speaking Caribbean Community (CARICOM) country of Haiti, where criminal gangs are seeking to overthrow the government following the assassination of President Jovenel Moise in 2021, the security crisis continues to retard political renewal and economic recovery.

“Still, preparations for a return to constitutional government are moving forward, even with great difficulty. But those efforts cannot succeed unless security improves, particularly in the areas containing more than half of Haiti’s electorate.”

She said that as a result, Barbados supports the full deployment that has been long-promised and the renewal of the mandate of the 5,500 Gang Suppression Force (GSF), a multinational security mission authorised by the United Nations Security Council to combat armed gangs in Haiti.

“Let me remind you that it was in 2022 that this recent, more heightened state of insecurity began with the fuel riots. Enough is enough. At the same time, we thank all member states who have contributed in whatever way to helping Haiti find its path.”

Mottley said that this includes the three-member CARICOM Eminent Persons Group (EPG), chaired by the former St. Lucia prime minister Dr. Kenny Anthony and including Bruce Golding and Perry Christie, the former prime ministers of Jamaica and The Bahamas respectively.

She said that EPG has been helping to build consensus in Haiti and maintain engagement with key international partners.

Mottley said that the region is also “deeply concerned” by the worsening humanitarian pressures facing the people of Cuba as the United States, which has in place a decades old trade and economic embargo against Havana, has in recent months stepped its programme of seeking to remove the government on the island.

The aggressive strategy, led by the Donald Trump administration has pushed the island into an unprecedented humanitarian and economic crisis, and following Washington’s removal of the Nicolás Maduro government in Venezuela, it has completely halted Venezuelan oil shipments to Cuba, cutting off the island’s primary energy lifeline.

“Too many people are suffering. Restrictions on trade, finance and access to fuel are intensifying hardship not only for Cuban citizens, but also for all others who study and live there,” Mottley said, adding that Barbados has, each year, opposed the use of the embargo and other unilateral coercive measures against Cuba.

“As always, we call for constructive engagement. This must be grounded in dialogue, sovereign equality and respect for international law. “

Mottley said that Barbados was also extending its continued solidarity to the people of Venezuela as they recover from the devastating double earthquakes in June and that Bridgetown remains committed to supporting the Soyth American country’s longer-term recovery.

“A stable, sovereign, peaceful and democratic Venezuela is vital to the security and prosperity of the wider Caribbean. In this regard, I take this opportunity to reiterate Barbados’ steadfast support to its sister CARICOM country of Guyana as it seeks to bring a peaceful resolution, through the International Court of Justice, to the long outstanding controversy with Venezuela.

“This is in the interest of the people of Guyana, Venezuela and the people of the wider Caribbean,” Mottley said, adding “the Caribbean must remain a Zone of Peace.”

In her address, Mottley said that on March 25th this year, the United nations adopted a “historic resolution” where the overwhelming majority of states acknowledged the truth that the trafficking of enslaved African and Racialised Chattel Enslavement of Africans was the gravest crime against humanity.

“Yes, we in Barbados painfully know this reality. Regrettably we still carry the scars.

I have reminded us that it was my country that passed the first Slave Code in 1661. Others followed, including the infamous Code Noir of 1685. It was only repealed this year; hence the wounds are still raw.”

She said Barbados accepts the moral responsibility of removing the cross of slavery with its horrific consequences, adding “we must effect healing through reparatory justice. It is the right thing to do.”

She said in July, Caribbean leaders approved the revised CARICOM Ten Point Plan for Reparatory Justice, telling the global community “for the Caribbean, for Africa and for all of those countries concerned, the honest engagement must begin.

“We do not ask for reparations without accepting responsibility for our own self-repair which we have undertaken for decades. I want to be very clear about this Mr President. Let there be no doubt.

“The mindset that established, justified and sustained slavery is the same mindset that sustains the iniquities and inequities within the power structures of this very institution and within the international financial architecture. The same mindset that caused a global map to remain grossly inaccurate for centuries.”

news.title: India, Russia reaffirm commitment to 'special, privileged' strategic partnership
news.text: Digital Desk | United Nations, Sep 26 (IANS) India and Russia reaffirmed their commitment to "the special and privileged" strategic partnership during a meeting between External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar and Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov here, according to Moscow's foreign ministry. "The sides reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening the special and privileged Russia-India Strategic Partnership and close coordination at the UN, G20 and BRICS", the ministry said in an X post after the Friday meeting. EAM Jaishankar wrote on X that they "exchanged views on a number of ongoing issues. Also took stock of our bilateral and BRICS cooperation". Lavrov had visited India earlier this month for the BRICS summit along with Russia's President Vladimir Putin. US President Donald Trump has invited Putin to the G20 Summit of industrialised and emerging economies in December, which Prime Minister Narendra Modi is also expected to attend. At his meeting with Putin at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Kyrgyzstan late last month, PM Modi firmly asked him to end the Ukraine War in the name of humanity. EAM Jaishankar had met Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on Monday. He wrote on X tersely after the meeting that they "focused on developments over the past few weeks", while Sybiha said more explicitly that they discussed "peace efforts". Neither EAM Jaishankar nor the Russian ministry mentioned the Ukraine War as a topic of discussion in the Lavrov meeting. But EAM Jaishankar cryptically mentioned their discussion covered a "number of ongoing issues". As founding members, India and Russia have often coordinated positions on issues ranging from reforming global financial institutions to technology transfer and the energy transition. The meeting also highlights India’s active diplomatic calendar at UNGA, where EAM Jaishankar has been holding bilateral talks with counterparts from multiple countries. His engagements are expected to focus on strengthening partnerships, addressing global challenges such as climate change and terrorism, and reinforcing India’s role as a voice for the Global South.

news.title: Bill Clinton who had an affair in office admits there were times he wanted to ban the press - but didn’t
news.text:
Bill Clinton, whose presidency was thrown into turmoil over an affair with a young staffer, has admitted there were times he wanted to ban the press from the White House, as President Donald Trump recently did, but he refrained. 

“There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps,” the former president said to laughter at the Clinton Global Initiative summit earlier this week. “And there's a reason we have a constitution. Because none of us are immune from being pissed off."

Clinton was likely referring to his affair with Monica Lewinsky, which rocked Washington in the late 1990s and — following allegations of a cover-up by the then-president — led to his impeachment in December 1998. He was later acquitted by the Senate.

The Democrat’s comments came after Trump banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House because of unfavorable coverage. 

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” the president wrote on Truth Social last Friday.

Lewinsky was a 22-year-old intern at the White House when she began an affair with Clinton, who was nearly 30 years her senior and married to Hillary Clinton. 

Lewinsky recalled the moment the news of her clandestine relationship with the president broke during a February 2025 interview with Call Her Daddy podcast host Alex Cooper.

“I remember opening the door — and these were in the days where people would get a newspaper delivered and in D.C. it was always several like The [Washington] Post and The New York Times — I remember seeing my name above the fold…and looking down the hall and seeing the exact same newspaper outside everybody else's door,” Lewinsky said. 

“It was shocking, it was terrifying and I didn't actually know how to process anything and really it was a moment where life as I knew it was over.”

Trump has faced his own fair share of scandals that the media has covered, including two impeachments and multiple criminal indictments — one of which involved a hush money payment to a porn star. 

His administration has also been criticized for its massive, hardline immigration crackdown and its war in Iran, which has caused gas prices to soar. 

Unlike Clinton during the height of his sex scandal, when Trump faced scrutiny from the press, he decided to ban several outlets from covering his daily activities, calling them “fake news.” 

CNN, MS NOW and Politico subsequently filed a lawsuit to regain access to the White House, arguing the ban violated their First Amendment rights.

In an early morning ruling Thursday, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the Trump administration to temporarily reinstate the outlets’ press badges. 

But the outlets were still denied access at times, causing their journalists to reportedly miss Chinese President Xi Jinping’s arrival at the White House for a state Dinner Thursday. 

“The big question is — is this going to continue? Are we not going to be credentialed into these daily events?” MS NOW White House reporter Laura Barrón-López, who said she was not allowed to cover Xi’s arrival, told network host Symone Sanders Townsend.
news.summary: The Democrat was at the center of one of Washington’s biggest scandals during his presidency after news about an affair with intern Monica Lewinsky broke in the 1990s
news.author: Rachel Dobkin

news.title: Trump uses contested power to cut nearly $1B US in Congress-approved spending
news.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump is cancelling nearly $1 billion US in spending approved by Congress, the White House announced on Friday, using a rare and contested power to axe funding for immigrant services and diversity-focused initiatives.

Trump's Office of Management and Budget (OMB) described the funding cut as focused on "the most harmful government spending."

Most of the cuts are focused on services for immigrants, including non-profits that serve refugees and unaccompanied minors accused of being in the country illegally. The administration says the funds are no longer necessary because illegal border crossings have diminished considerably. 

Also targeted for cuts were a Department of Education program for migrant students; a Department of Justice office focused on reducing racial tensions; a business development initiative for minority entrepreneurs; housing counselling services from the Housing and Urban Development Department; and a series of grants from the Health and Human Services Department that the administration called "outright harmful and blatantly ideological." 

A White House news release announcing the funding cuts notes some of the organizations are led by people who worked in the administration of former president Barack Obama, a Democrat. 

Trump's move was condemned by Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican in a tough re-election campaign and chair of the Senate Committee on Appropriations. 

Carney's comments over possibility of U.S. invasion reveal how contingency plans are always in placeTrump's top trade envoy says U.S. 'comfortable' with state of relationship with Canada

Collins said in a statement that the action came without warning or consultation. She also said she would work to address with colleagues "these illegal actions."

"… It is a usurpation of Congress's appropriations powers," Collins said. "OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding."

'Pocket rescission' manoeuvre

Under federal law, Congress has 45 days to review the president's proposed spending cuts before they take effect. But Trump made that all but impossible by announcing them with just five days left in the federal fiscal year and the House out of session through the November midterm elections. 

The Government Accountability Office — the independent, non-partisan watchdog agency that works for Congress — says the manoeuvre, known as a "pocket rescission," is illegal.

Collins called it the latest attempt by OMB to "undermine Congress's constitutional power of the purse."

A year ago, Trump issued a pocket rescission for the first time in nearly 50 years by blocking $4.9 billion US in congressionally approved foreign aid. The U.S. Supreme Court declined to block those rescissions, saying Trump's authority over foreign affairs weighed heavily in its decision. This year, Trump is targeting domestic spending. 

The use of a pocket rescission fits a broader pattern by the Trump administration to exact greater control over the U.S. government, eroding the power of Congress.

Essentially the last pocket rescission occurred in 1977 when then-president Jimmy Carter rescinded it. The Trump administration argues it’s a legally permissible tool, despite some murkiness, since Carter had initially proposed the clawback well ahead of the 45-day deadline.

The administration has also fired federal workers, imposed a historic increase in tariffs, and started the war in Iran without going through Congress, putting the burden on the judicial branch to determine the limits of presidential power. 

'Theft from the American people': senator

Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, the lead Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, described the White House action as "theft from the American people, plain and simple."

"These are funds Congress has delivered on a bipartisan basis and should be helping people — not cut off by a president more focused on building a ballroom than investing in families," Murray said.

Murray said in recent spending negotiations, Democrats fought to include language to prevent the administration from usurping Congress's power on spending decisions, but Republicans have declined to go along.

"While Trump spends tax dollars on ads promoting himself, Congress needs to reassert its powers to help people, and it's past time Republicans join us in that fight," she said.

In addition to immigrant services, the White House said it was rescinding $70 million US for what it called "woke" international education programs, $28 million US in grant funding for Health and Human Services research programs, and $9 million US in debt relief for foreign countries that fund climate change policies. Another $10 million US was being withheld from a minority business development program.
news.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump is cancelling nearly $1 billion US in spending approved by Congress, the White House announced on Friday, using a rare and contested power to axe funding for immigrant services and diversity-focused initiatives.

news.title: Trump administration to meet Ukraine assistance deadline
news.text: Washington - The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump has made legally binding commitments to spend almost all of the $400 million Congress approved for military aid to Ukraine late last year, ensuring that the money will not expire on Sept. 30, according to three sources familiar with the plan.As of early this week, $307 million of the $400 million of the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative (USAI) funding had been obligated, said the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity, and the administration plans to lock in the remaining $93 million before the fiscal year ends on Sept. 30.The Pentagon, which oversees the USAI program, declined to comment for this story.
